title: Shapes with an Abstract Base Class
oneLiner: Fill in Circle, Rectangle and Square classes that inherit from an abstract Shape, each with its own name and area.
keyTakeaway: An abstract base class fixes what every subclass must provide (here a name and an area) and lets code work with a list of Shape without caring which kind each one is. Reuse by inheritance where it's a real "is a": a Square is a Rectangle whose sides are equal.
explanation:
The starter code has an abstract class Shape with an abstract Name and an abstract Area. Complete three subclasses: Circle(radius) with name "circle" and area π × radius²; Rectangle(width, height) with name "rectangle" and area width × height; and Square(side) with name "square" and area side². Use Math.PI in C# and math.pi in Python.

Each test is a list of shape descriptions such as "circle 2" or "rect 2 3". The checker builds one of your shapes for each, then reports every shape's name and its area rounded to 2 decimal places, so ["circle 1", "rect 2 3"] expects [["circle", 3.14], ["rectangle", 6]].

In C#, override the abstract members with override, and pass Square's side to Rectangle's constructor with : base(side, side), then override Name. In Python, inherit from Shape, write name() and area() methods, and call super().__init__(side, side) in Square. The checker in Python also refuses any shape that doesn't inherit from Shape, and Python itself refuses to create a subclass that leaves an abstract method unwritten.

visualizationSteps.message: Three different classes, all held as Shape. The checker only calls Name and Area.
Square is a Rectangle with both sides 3, so it can reuse Rectangle's Area: 3 × 3 = 9. Only its Name differs.
One loop, three behaviours: that's polymorphism.

complexity.note: Each shape stores one or two numbers and computes its area with a fixed number of operations. Building the n shapes in a test is O(n) overall.
